sec.title: Background
sec.p: Plant height-related traits are important for optimal architecture and grain yield in wheat (Triticum aestivum L.). In this study, association analysis based on single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and structural chromosome variations (SCVs) was performed on eight plant height-related traits in a natural population of 281 accessions. Linkage analysis was applied to two populations: a doubled haploid (DH) population of 180 lines derived from the cross ‘Jinchun 7 × Jinmai 919’ and a recombinant inbred line (RIL) population of 165 F10 lines from the cross ‘DH 118 × Jinmai 919’ to verify the genetic effects of stable major loci.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: In the natural population, plant height (PH) varied from 69.6 cm to 136.6 cm. PH and internode length decreased gradually across years of release, but the selection pressure varied among PH components. The uppermost internode length decreased the fastest across years of release, while spike length (SL) increased across the same timeframe. A total of 22 SNP loci and 19 SCV loci were detected by association mapping, which collectively explaining 3.8–12.5% variation, including five novel loci (QPH.sxau-2A, QSL.sxau-7B.2, QSEL.sxau-5A, QLI3.sxau-7A, and QLI5.sxau-2B). SNPs and SCVs co-localized to 14 marker-trait associations (MTAs), which explained 3.2–12.5% of the phenotypic variation, including QSL.sxau-7B.1 (SCV locus Mr7B-13), which was verified in the DH population. The phenotypic values for PH and internode length decreased and SL increased with an increasing number of favorable SNPs and SCVs allelic variation. In particular, QPH.sxau-2A was identified by using association and linkage analysis, with its fine mapping narrowing the functional region down to a 41.8 Mb genomic interval, containing three candidate genes TraesCS2A02G309300, TraesCS2A02G288000, and TraesCS2A02G288300.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Genotype emerged as the primary factor influencing plant-height-related trait variation. Association mapping detected 22 SNP loci and 19 SCV loci, and these loci exhibited additive effects. This study identifies novel loci for the genetic basis of plant height-related traits.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) is a staple food source for more than 35% of the global population, contributing 21% of total caloric intake and 20% of dietary protein [1]. Plant height (PH) is an important agronomic trait for morphogenesis and grain yield formation. An optimal PH is a prerequisite for attaining the desired yield in wheat breeding programs. Excessively tall or short PH may lead to lodging or reduced biomass and yield. Therefore, different countries and ecological regions have adopted distinct criteria for PH in wheat breeding programs, with PH consistently recognized as a key trait in genetic breeding efforts.

PH is a quantitative trait controlled by multiple genes. At present, more than 800 quantitative trait loci (QTL) for PH have been identified using linkage mapping and association analysis, which are distributed across the 21 chromosomes of wheat [2, 3]. A total of 27 dwarfing genes have been officially named and 12 key genes have been successfully cloned, which are Rht1, Rht2, Rht3, Rht8, Rht10, Rht11, Rht12, Rht13, Rht17, Rht18, Rht24, and Rht25 [3–6]. Rht1, Rht2, Rht8, Rht24, and Rht25 have been broadly used in breeding [4, 7, 8]. Despite this, our understanding of PH-related QTL and genes remains incomplete. Therefore, it is essential to identify PH-related QTL and genes in available germplasm, elucidate their genetic effects, and facilitate the efficient utilization of these loci to improve plant architecture and agricultural productivity.

Morphologically, PH is determined by spike length (SL) and the lengths of five to six internodes. Previous studies on QTL associated with PH mostly focused on the SL and the length of uppermost internode (UI) [9–14]. For example, Yu et al. [10] identified 10 QTL for UI and six QTL for SL from two recombinant inbred lines (RILs). QSEL.sicau-2–5A for spike extension length was found to be independent of PH [15]. In addition, QTL for other PH components (PHCs) have also been investigated. For example, a total of 86 QTL for PH, SL, and internode length were identified in a natural population [16]. A genome-wide association study (GWAS) of the UI and the length of each internode was performed using 306 wheat accessions worldwide, revealing 11 stable QTL across three environments [17]. Furthermore, a total of 16 QTL for the second internode length from the top to the fifth internode length from the top were detected in the RIL population [18]. However, a few major-effect loci of PHCs stable across multiple environments was identified, and the genetic effects of these loci on PH remain were unclear. Therefore, identifying stable PHC loci across multiple environments and elucidating their genetic effects are crucial for optimizing wheat plant architecture through rational internode configuration.

Studies on QTL mapping for PH have revealed that certain QTL/genes associated with PH also influence on yield-related traits. The gene TaPRR95 has been shown to regulate PH and shorten the heading date [19]. The favorable haplotype of TaDEP1 can increase grain length (GL), grain width, grain thickness, and thousand-grain weight (TGW), while reducing PH [1]. QGns.cib-2B.1 for grain number per spike (GNS) has been reported to reduce PH by 3.9%, elongated SL by 8.6%, and increased GNS by 5.8% [20]. The Rht1 and Rht2 genes promote spike development, increase tiller number and GNS, while reducing PH [21]. The Rht8 could enhance the yield by about 9.7% and reduce PH [22]. The Rht4 reduced PH by shortening the length of each internode, but also educed TGW and GNS [23]. Additionally, the length of PHCs has been found to be negatively correlated with TGW, while positively correlated with individual plant yield [24]. The locus QSnl-4D has been reported to regulate the length of two basal internodes and UI while also affecting GL and TGW [25]. In conclusion, the genetic effects of PHCs on yield-related traits remain inconclusive. Therefore, systematic analysis of QTL and genes underlying different PHCs, along with screening for suitable genes, will facilitate precise modification of PH and regulation of yield formation.

Nucleic acid marker is main marker for using association and linkage analysis, to identify the QTLs and genes for PH [26–28]. Structural variation (SV) is an important source of genetic variation and affects more nucleotides than SNPs, often with larger or comparable effects relative to SNPs [29, 30]. SV has various variant types, including presence/absence variations (PAV), copy number variations (CNV), inversions, translocations, and complex rearrangements. CNV of the VRN-A1 gene has played a critical role in the transition from spring-type to winter-type wheat, and the absence of the Pina gene has been significantly associated with increased grain hardness [31]. The effect of the translocation line T 1BL‧1RS on PH and biomass has been well established. However, structural chromosome variations (SCVs) related to PHCs have not been reported. Thus, identifying SCVs for plant height-related traits and their genetic effects in different populations is an urgent task in the progress of molecular improvement for further wheat breeding programs.

In the present study, we employed SNPs and SCVs combined with association and linkage analysis to (1) analyze the variations of plant height-related traits in a natural population, (2) explore the relationship between the plant height-related traits and yield-related traits such as SN, GNS, and TGW, (3) identify stable loci associated with plant height-related traits, and (4) verify the genetic effects of identified major and novel loci in genetic populations. This research is expected to provide important genetic loci for molecular marker-assisted selection (MAS) breeding.

sec.title: Plant materials
sec.p: Four wheat germplasm sets (Panel-1 to Panel-4) were employed in this study. Among them, Panel-1 was used for GWAS, while Panel-2, Panel-3, and Panel-4 were used to validate QTL identified in the GWAS panel.

list-item.p: Panel-1 consisted of 281 hexaploid wheat accessions from China, which included 40 landraces (LC) and 241 modern cultivars (MC). The 40 landraces were obtained from the Chinese Wheat Core Collection, while the 241 modern cultivars have represented 83% of the officially approved cultivars released in the past 80 years, including 127 irrigated cultivars (IC) and 114 dryland cultivars (DC) [32].

Panel-2 consisted of 180 doubled haploid (DH) lines derived from a cross between Jinchun 7 and Jinmai 919. Jinchun 7 (JC, released in 1982) and the drought-tolerant cultivar Jinmai 919 (JM, released in 2018) are from Shanxi Province, China. There were significant differences in plant height-related traits between the two cultivars.

Panel-3 consisted of the 165 F10 RILs from a cross between DH 118 (Yaomai 33) and Jinmai 919. DH 118 is a high-yielding irrigated cultivar and was bred by the Institute of Wheat Research at Shanxi Agricultural University.

Panel-4 was a secondary mapping population. One residual heterozygous line (RHL) was identified from the F10 RILs (DH 118 × Jinmai 919), and then a population consisting of 542 lines was developed by self-crossing the RHL. The corresponding heterozygous lines were then used for continuous self-crossing to identify the key recombinant lines (RLs).

sec.title: Field trials
sec.p: Panel-1 was grown in Linfen (36°13’N, 111°34’E) in Shanxi Province of China in 2019–2020 and 2020–2021. It was planted in a 2 m2 plot with six rows of 1.5 m in length. The rows were 0.25 m apart and 50 seeds were evenly planted per row. Each plot was harvested in turn using a plot harvester. The irrigation regimes were as follows: once (I1) at the overwintering stage, twice (I2) at the overwintering and jointing stage, and three times (I3) at the overwintering, jointing and booting stage. Irrigation was applied at a rate of 700 m3·ha−1 per application. The three irrigation regimes were applied in randomized complete blocks with two replications in two consecutive years, providing six environments: E1 (I1, 2020), E2 (I2, 2020), E3 (I3, 2020), E4 (I1, 2021), E5 (I2, 2021), and E6 (I3, 2021).

The three plant panels (Panel-2, Panel-3, and Panel-4) were grown at three experimental stations in Shanxi Province: the Yaodu station in Linfen (YD, 36°08’N, 111°52’E), the Hancun station in Linfen (HC, 36°25’N, 111°67’E), and the Nanhua station in Yuncheng (NH, 34°35’N, 110°15’E) during the 2019–2020 and 2020–2021 seasons. Each panel was subjected to two irrigation regimes: well-watered (WW) and rain-fed (RF) at each station and in each growing season. The field experiment followed a randomized complete block design with three replications per panel per station. Each experimental plot consisted of two rows, each 1.5 m long and spaced 0.3 m apart, with 21 seeds sown per row.

sec.title: Phenotypic evaluation
sec.p: A total of 18 agronomic traits were evaluated in this study. The heading date (HD) was recorded from mid- to late-April to early May. Ten days before harvest, 12 traits were measured, which included plant height-related traits and spike-related traits. Plant height-related traits were categorized into PH and PHCs. The PHCs comprised spike length (SL), spike extension length (SEL), and the lengths of five successive internodes from the top of the stem: uppermost internode (UI), second internode (LI2), third internode (LI3), fourth internode (LI4), and fifth internode (LI5). Spike-related traits included spikelet number per spike (SN), grain number per spike (GNS), basal sterile spikelet number (BSSN), and top sterile spikelet number (TSSN). After harvest, grain length (GL), grain width (GW), grain thickness (GT), thousand-grain weight (TGW), and grain yield (GY) were measured. Each trait was measured on 10 wheat plants randomly selected from the middle of each plot.

sec.title: Cytological analysis
sec.p: Chromosome preparations and the FISH procedures were performed as described by Zhao et al. [33]. The probes used in the present study were modified versions of ONPM#7 [34]. The pAs1-1, pAs1-3, pAs1-4, pAs1-6, AFA-3, AFA-4, pSc119.2-1, 5S-1, and 5S-2 were modified with 6-carboxytetramethylrhodamine (TAMRA), whereas the BSCL135-1, BSCL135-2 and (GAA)10 were modified with 6 carboxyfluorescein (FAM). All oligonucleotides were synthesized and modified by General Biosystems (Chuzhou, China). For karyotyping, 5–8 plants per line and 3–5 cells per plant were analyzed. Cells with a full complement of chromosomes and good dispersion were selected for karyotype analysis.

sec.title: Genomic DNA extraction and GWAS
sec.p: Genomic DNA was extracted using the Cetyltrimethylammonium Bromide (CTAB) method [35]. High-throughput genotyping was performed using a 15 K SNP panel from the MOL-BREEDING Company, and a total of 9793 high-quality SNPs were identified for GWAS [35]. The allelic diversity and genetic structure of 281 wheat cultivars were reported in Zheng et al. [35]. TASSEL 5.0 was used to examine the associations of the SNPs with the phenotypic variations of plant height-related traits in E1, E2, E3, E4, E5, E6, and the best linear unbiased prediction (BLUP) datasets. The SNPs-trait association was tested using the mixed linear model (MLM), with a threshold of log10(p) > 3 used to define significant marker-trait associations (MTAs). The loci detected in three or more environments were considered stable loci.

Karyotypes were determined using ONPM#7 FISH to identify SCV alleles at 230 loci. Using the high-resolution karyotype of Chinese Spring as a reference, chromosomal variations caused by heterochromatin were physically mapped and then used as mapping markers [32]. The allelic diversity and genetic structure of 281 wheat cultivars based on SCV were reported in Zhao et al. [32]. The SCV-MTAs were tested using TASSEL 5.0 and the MTAs with a threshold of p < 0.05 were considered significant [32]. The extended region where the LD between nearby SNPs and the peak SNP decayed to r2 = 0.2 was defined as the local LD-based QTL interval [36]. The Manhattan graph visualization was completed by the CMplot package in R (https://github.com/YinLiLin/CMplot).

sec.title: Linkage analysis of DH and RIL population
sec.p: The DH population, RIL population, and the parents were genotyped with the Infinium wheat SNP 90 K iSelect assay (Illumina Inc., San Diego, CA, United States) developed by the International Wheat SNP Consortium [37]. QTL were detected using WinQTLCart version 2.5 based on the composite interval mapping (CIM). The LOD threshold for QTL detection was determined by using 1000 permutations at p < 0.05, and the threshold LOD value was 2.5. Stable QTL were detected in at least three datasets including the BLUP dataset. The chromosome location map of QTL was drawn in MapChart software. To determine the physical position of the identified QTL regions, a BLAST search in WheatOmics2.16 (http://wheatomics.sdau.edu.cn/) was performed to align the sequences of the peak SNP markers associated with QTL and their flanking markers.

sec.title: Marker development and PCR amplification
sec.p: Flanking sequences of SNPs near the QPH.sxau-2A on chromosome 2A was used for BLAST search with IWGSC RefSeq v2.1 (https://urgi.versailles.inra.fr/blast) to obtain the physical position of QPH.sxau-2A. According to the results of resequencing (DH 118 × Jinmai 919, unpublished data), the SNPs and InDels were identified for developing saturated markers within the target region. The polymorphic sequences containing InDel (> 3 bp) were converted to PCR-based markers using PrimerServer (http://202.194.139.32/PrimerServer/) [37], and the KASP primers were designed with Polymarker (http://www.polymarker.info/). The PCR was performed in a total volume of 25 µL with the initial denaturation at 94 °C for 4 min, followed by 35 cycles at 94 °C for 45 s, annealing for 45 s, and extension at 72 °C for 30 s–3 min, and a final extension for 10 min. The annealing temperatures and extension times varied according to the primer set and the size of the PCR products. After amplification, the PCR products were separated using 8% denaturing polyacrylamide gels and stained with AgNO₃ and visualized under UV light.

sec.title: Data analysis
sec.p: In order to minimize the environmental effects, the BLUP values across different datasets were conducted using JMP PRO. The broad-sense heritability (H2) value was calculated using the formula H2 = VG/(VG + VE/r), where VG was the genotypic variance, VE was the environment variables, and r was the number of replications [38]. The BLUP values of the six environments in Panel-1 were used as variables, and the IBM SPSS Statistics 25 software was used for one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) and correlation analysis (the Pearson method was selected for calculating the correlation coefficient). The simple correlation coefficients were partitioned into direct and indirect effects using conventional path coefficient analysis based on the stepwise multiple regression model.

sec.title: Phenotypic variation of plant height-related traits
sec.p: The plant height-related traits were mainly affected by heredity with the heritability larger than 0.88 (Supplemental Table S1). Plant height-related traits exhibited extensive variation, with coefficients of variation (CV) ranging from 11.9 to 37.2%, among which the CV for PH was 17.7%. In PHCs, SL displayed the smallest CV at 11.9%, and LI4, LI5, and SEL showed notably higher variability, with CVs of 27.6%, 29.7%, and 37.2%, respectively. Plant height-related traits differed across different ecological regions. The PH in the Yellow-Huai River Valleys Facultative Wheat region of China was generally shorter (90.3 cm on average), significantly lower than that in the Northern Spring Wheat region (105.2 cm) and the Northern Winter Wheat region (100.0 cm). For the PHCs, SL in the Northern Spring Wheat region was significantly higher than that in other two wheat regions. LI4 in the Yellow-Huai River Valleys Facultative Wheat Region was significantly lower than that in the Northern Spring Wheat Region and the Northern Winter Wheat Region. Additionally, SEL, UI, LI2, LI3, and LI5 showed the following order: Northern Spring Wheat region > Northern Winter Wheat region > Yellow-Huai River Valleys Facultative Wheat region (Supplemental Fig. S1).

There were differences in plant height-related traits among different cultivar types. The average PH of landraces was 125.5 cm, which was significantly higher than that of modern cultivars (94.9 cm). Among the modern cultivars, the PH of dryland cultivars was about 10.0 cm higher than that of irrigated ones (Supplemental Table S1, Fig. 1a). Using the landraces as reference, the SL of modern cultivars increased significantly by 1.3 cm, with no significant difference in SL observed between irrigated and dryland cultivars. The SEL, UI, LI2, LI3, LI4, and LI5 in modern cultivars were significantly reduced by 5.3 cm, 6.2 cm, 5.9 cm, 6.1 cm, 5.6 cm, and 4.1 cm, respectively; and those of the dryland cultivars were greater than those of the irrigated cultivars (Supplemental Table S1).

sec.p: After long-term natural and artificial selection, the PH and internode length decreased gradually across years of release, but the selection pressure varied among the PHCs. Among the PHCs, the UI decreased the fastest across years of release. However, the proportions of SL and UI in overall PH increased in modern cultivars compared with landraces (Fig. 1b). Specifically, the proportions of both SL and UI in PH were significantly higher in irrigated cultivars than that in dryland cultivars (Supplemental Table S2). Conversely, the phenotypic values of SEL, LI4, and LI5 and their proportion in PH showed a decreasing trend across years of release. Relative to landraces, the proportions of SEL, LI4, and LI5 in modern cultivars decreased by 1.2%, 0.5%, and 0.6%, respectively (Fig. 1b, Supplemental Fig. S2). The proportion of LI4 to PH is higher in dryland cultivars than that in irrigated cultivars (Supplemental Table S2). There was no significant difference in the proportion of LI2 and LI3 between landraces and modern cultivars (Supplemental Fig. S2).

The SL and UI showed a significant positive correlation with PH (Fig. 1c, Supplemental Fig. S3a), whereas the proportion of SL and UI in PH exhibited a significant negative correlation with PH (Supplemental Fig. S3b). Both the SEL, LI4, LI5 and their proportions in PH were significantly positively correlated with PH, with the correlation coefficients of 0.8, 0.9, and 0.8 (0.4, 0.6, and 0.4), respectively (Supplemental Fig. S3b). Moreover, LI2 and LI3 were also significantly positively correlated with PH, with the strongest correlation observed for LI3 (r = 0.9, Supplemental Fig. S3a). Path analysis revealed the direct effect order of each PHC as LI3 > SEL > LI4 > UI > LI5 > SL > LI2, with the largest direct path coefficient between LI3 and PH at 0.4.

Plant height-related traits, important indicator for evaluating wheat growth and development, showed that the effects of irrigation methods on plant height-related traits varied with cultivar types. In I2 and I3 environments, the PH of landraces and modern cultivars was significantly higher than that in I1. All PHCs in modern cultivars demonstrated significant sensitivity to water regimes (p < 0.05), while among landraces, only UI, LI2, LI3, and LI4 showed statistically significant difference under varying irrigation treatments. Specifically, trait values under I2 and I3 were significantly higher than under I1, with no significant differences between I2 and I3 (Supplemental Table S1). SEL of dryland cultivars showed no significant differences across water treatments; however, SL and LI5 exhibited significantly higher values under I3 compared to I1 (with no differences between I2 and I1). A similar pattern was observed in irrigated cultivars for LI4 and LI5 (i.e., significant differences only between I3 and I1). Trait values of UI, LI2, LI3, and LI4 in dryland cultivars, and SL, SEL, UI, LI2, and LI3 in irrigated cultivars were significantly higher under I2 and I3 irrigation regimes than that under I1.

sec.title: Relationship between plant height-related traits and yield-related traits
sec.p: Plant height-related traits had a significant influence on yield-related traits (Supplemental Fig. S3a). In landraces, PH and internode length were significantly associated with yield-related traits, including spike-related traits (GNS, SN, and BSSN) and kernel weight related traits (GL, GW, GT, and TGW). Specifically, LI5 was associated with GY, while PH, LI2, LI3, and LI4 showed significant associations with TGW, with LI2 additionally associated to GNS. Similar to landraces, TGW in modern cultivars was correlated with PH, LI2, LI3, and LI4. By contrast, GNS in modern cultivars was associated not only with LI2 but also with PH, SEL, UI, LI4, and LI5 (Supplemental Fig. S3a). These results indicate that plant height-related traits are critical in regulating yield formation.

sec.title: Association analysis between SNPs and plant height-related traits
sec.p: Association analysis between eight plant height-related traits and SNP markers was performed using the MLM model. A total of 22 stable loci were identified, located on chromosomes 1A, 1B, 2A, 2B, 2D, 3A, 4B, 5A, 6B, 6D, 7A, and 7B. The contribution of phenotypic variation ranged from 3.8 to 12.5% (Table 1, Supplemental Fig. S4a). Four of these stable loci were significantly associated with PH, explaining 3.8–7.4% of phenotypic variation. Among these, QPH.sxau-1A, QPH.sxau-2D, and QPH.sxau-6D have been previously reported to be associated with PH (Table 1), while QPH.sxau-2A was identified as a novel locus. A total of 18 stable loci were detected for PHCs, with QSL.sxau-7B.1 explaining the largest contribution of phenotypic variation (12.5%). Among these, nine loci have been previously reported to be associated with plant height-related traits, whereas four loci (QSL.sxau-7B.2, QSEL.sxau-5A, QLI3.sxau-7A, and QLI5.sxau-2B) have not been reported previously (Table 1).

sec.p: The peak markers of QPH.sxau-2D, QLI3.sxau-2D, and QLI4.sxau-2D were found to share the same physical location, which encompassed Rht8. The QPH.sxau-1A locus associated with PH was also stably detected in LI2, as was the QPH.sxau-6D across LI2, LI3, and LI4. Moreover, the QLI2.sxau-4B locus was associated with LI3 and contained Rht1 (Table 1; Fig. 2a).

sec.title: Association analysis between SCVs and plant height-related traits
sec.p: The ONPM#7 could identify 230 structural variation loci across 21 chromosomes of wheat, providing a simple and efficient tool for the identification of SCVs [32]. In this study, the association analysis between SCVs and eight plant height-related traits was performed. A total of 19 stable loci were detected on chromosomes 1A, 1B, 1D, 2A, 2B, 2D, 3A, 3B, 4A, 6A, and 7B, which explained 4.2–9.3% of the phenotypic variation. Six SCVs associated with PH were mapped to chromosomes 1B, 2B, and 3B. For PHCs, LI2 was significantly correlated with 7 out of 19 SCVs. The highest R2 value (9.3%) was found for the association between Mg1A-3 and UI, which was confirmed in three datasets.

Nine SCVs were found significantly associated with two or more plant height-related traits, among which six SCVs showed effects on both the PH and the PHCs. Specifically, Mg1B-1 and Mr1B-3 were significantly associated with PH and were stably detected involving LI4, LI5, and LI3, respectively. It is noteworthy that T 1BL‧1RS was stably detected to be associated with PH, LI2, and LI3. Mg2B-13 simultaneously affected PH, LI2, LI4, and LI5. Additionally, Mr3B-10 was found associated with PH, LI3, LI4, and LI5. Mr2B-12 significantly influenced PH and PHCs but not SL, explaining 4.4–9.1% of the phenotypic variation. Mr1A-1 was significantly associated with SEL and UI, contributing to phenotypic variation ranging from 4.3 to 6.4%. Mg3B-11 affected both LI2 and UI, while Mr2A-9 was significantly associated with LI3 and SEL (Table 2). A total of 10 SCVs, including Mr3A-3, Mr3A-4, and Mg1A-3, were identified as PH-independent loci. Specifically, Mr3A-3, Mr3A-4, Mr7B-13, and Mg6A-8 were significantly associated with SL, whereas Mg1A-3 and Mg1A-7 were significantly associated with UI. Furthermore, Mr2D-7, 4AS‧4AL-1DS, and 1DL‧1DS-4AL were associated with LI2, whereas Mr3B-7 was associated with LI5.

sec.title: Positive selection for favored SCVs in historical Chinese wheat breeding program
sec.p: The frequency of favored SCVs across years of release indicated an evolutionary trend. Notably, the frequency of favored SCVs for PH increased from 23.8% in the 1940 s to 57.4% in the 2010 s (Supplemental Table S3, Fig. 2b). PHCs also showed a similar trend. Specifically, the frequency of favored SCVs for LI3 increased most rapidly from 15.0% in the 1940 s to 61.5% in the 2010 s, followed by LI4 and LI5. Conversely, the frequency of favored SCVs for SL increased slowly across years of release (Supplemental Table S3, Supplemental Fig. S4b). As the frequency of favored SCVs for PH and internode length increased, the corresponding average values of these traits decreased. The increased frequency of favored SCVs was accompanied by increased SL across years of release. This indicates that the favored SCVs were positively selected in wheat breeding history, and the frequency of the favored SCVs was closely associated with the decrease in PH.

sec.title: Co-localization analysis of SNPs and SCVs
sec.p: A total of 14 MTAs were co-located via SNP and SCV marker association analysis (Supplemental Table S4). QSL.sxau-7B.1 and Mr7B-13 were significantly associated with SL (Fig. 3d-e), with a relatively high rate of phenotypic variation explained, which was consistent with prior studies [44]. It is notable that QLI5.sxau-1B (Mg1B-1) is a novel locus that was associated with LI5 and remained stable in multiple environments (Supplemental Table S4, Supplemental Fig. S5a-c). For QLI5.sxau-1B, the significant differences were observed among allelic variations, with HapCC exhibiting a LI5 that was 10.1% shorter than that of HapAA (Supplemental Fig. S5d). The remaining 12 co-located loci were detected in one or two environments, which together explaining 3.2–7.9% of the phenotypic variation, and these loci have been reported to be associated with PH or PHCs.

sec.title: Verification of genetic effect of QSL.sxau-7B.1
sec.p: Among the MTAs identified through SNPs and SCVs association analysis, the locus QSL.sxau-7B.1 (Mr7B-13) explained notably more SL phenotypic variation, and the favored allelic variation of this locus showed a positive effect on SL. This region of QSL.sxau-7B.1 coincides with what was previously reported by Guo et al. [44]. Due to the difference in SCV between Jinchun 7 and Jinmai 919 at QSL.sxau-7B.1 (Fig. 3a-c), we employed Panel-2 to verify the genetic effect of this locus. The result showed that the SL in HapJM lines (carrying Mr7B-13) was longer than that in HapJC lines (without Mr7B-13), suggesting the participation of the SCV polymorphic region in PH regulation.

sec.title: Distribution and additive effects of favored SNPs and SCVs
sec.p: To further investigate the distribution of favored SNPs and SCVs in Panel-1, we analyzed their frequencies in relation to plant height-related traits among the landraces and modern cultivars. In general, the frequencies of favored allelic variations at SNPs and SCVs in modern cultivars were significantly higher than those in landraces, except for a few cases (Fig. 4a). For PH, the proportion of favored allelic variations at nine loci (excluding QPH.sxau-1A) was significantly higher in modern cultivars than that in landraces. For PHCs, the favored allelic variations at four loci (QSL.sxau-2D, QSL.sxau-7B.2, Mg3A-3, and Mg6A-8) associated with SL exhibited a higher frequency in modern cultivars. In contrast, the frequency of favored allelic variations of QSL.sxau-6B, QSL.sxau-7B.1, QLI2.sxau-1A, QLI3.sxau-7A, 4AS‧4AL-1DS, 1DL‧1DS-4AL, and Mr3B-7 was lower in modern cultivars (< 10%). Additionally, the total number of favored allele variations in modern cultivars surpassed that in landraces (Fig. 4b, Supplemental Fig. S7a).

sec.p: The SNP markers and SSR markers are effective tools for MAS breeding. We used cytological markers to identify loci for plant height-related traits and found that favored SCVs had a significant additive effect (Supplemental Fig. S6). Also the phenotypic values for PH and internode length decreased and SL increased with an increasing number of favorable SNPs and SCVs. The cultivars containing 10 favored allelic variations reduced PH by an average of 29.9% (Fig. 4c). When comparing the cultivars with the lowest and highest number of favored allelic variations of SNPs and SCVs, SEL, UI, LI2, LI3, LI4, and LI5 each decreased by 57.6%, 18.2%, 17.3%, 24.0%, 43.2%, and 50.5%, and SL increased by 36.7% on average (Fig. 4c, Supplemental Fig. S7b). These results support the usefulness of SCVs as a new marker type in MAS breeding and demonstrate the efficacy of accumulating favored SNPs and SCVs for PH improvement.

sec.title: Fine mapping of QPH.sxau-2A and analysis of candidate genes
sec.p: The locus QPH.sxau-2A identified in Panel-1 was also detected in linkage analysis in the RIL population (DH 118 × Jinmai 919), with an initial mapping interval of 262.3 cM-284.0 cM (Fig. 5a-b). Homozygous lines exhibiting significant phenotypic differences in PH were self-crossed to construct a secondary mapping population for the fine mapping of QPH.sxau-2A. The functional region of QPH.sxau-2A was narrowed down to an interval of 41.8 Mb between InDel 6 and InDel 9 using ten markers from 491.8 Mb to 533.6 Mb (Fig. 5c-d). In the functional region of QPH.sxau-2A, a total of 223 annotated genes were identified. Previous research has shown that the development and formation of PH were affected by the genes encoding serine/threonine protein kinase, ethylene-responsive transcription factor, auxin response factor, glycosyltransferase, E3 ubiquitin protein ligase, MADS-box transcription factor, and F-box protein [47–49]. Based on this, a total of 32 candidate genes associated with PH were screened out (Fig. 5e). Among those with homologues annotations, three candidates were particularly noteworthy, i.e., TraesCS2A02G309300, TraesCS2A02G288000, and TraesCS2A02G288300. TraesCS2A02G309300 were annotated as homologous to rice OsARF19, a gene that positively regulates the elongation of basal internodes and leaves [50]. High RNA expression levels of this gene were observed in the stem and shoot apical meristem of the Chinese Spring. TraesCS2A02G288000 was found to encode an ethylene-responsive transcription factor homologous to rice OsERF1, which influences organ size and negatively regulates shoot growth [51]; notably high expression was detected in the peduncle of Chinese Spring. TraesCS2A02G288300 had the annotation of encoding a glycosyltransferase, with its rice homologous OsGT47A showing high expression in the stem [52]. In Chinese Spring, TraesCS2A02G288300 exhibited high RNA expression levels in the second internode, stem, and peduncle (Fig. 5e).

sec.title: Variation in plant height-related traits under selection pressure
sec.p: PH directly impacts wheat plant architecture and yield potential. Therefore, the identification and functional characterization of related QTL and genes have long been a central focus of international wheat research. Numerous genetic studies on PH have been reported, with research on PHCs primarily focused on mapping QTL for SL and UI [13, 14]. As key components of PH, PHCs directly determines plant morphology. Therefore, investigating the genetic mapping of PHCs in wheat is essential for breeding programs. In the present study, association and linkage analysis were used to map the QTL for eight plant height-related traits based on SNPs and SCVs. This research expected to provide theoretical basis and the genetic regulation of PH and PHCs.

Among the cultivars in this study, PH and internode length exhibited a gradual decrease across years of release, whereas SL showed a continuous increase. This trend indicates that the plant height-related traits have been constantly selected to enhance wheat resistance to lodging to improve yield during the breeding process. However, the selection pressure varied among PHCs. The UI showed the most rapid decrease across years of release, while the proportion of UI to the PH increased across the same timeframe. A significant difference in the UI to PH ratio was observed between landraces and modern cultivars, which can be plausibly explained by shorter UI lowering the crop’s center of mass, thereby enhancing lodging resistance. Notably, as the important structure that connects stem and spike, the UI not only determines the extension of spike from the sheath, but also serves as a key channel for the remobilization of photosynthetic assimilates to the grain [13]. At late filling stage, the accumulating photosynthetic products such as glucose, fructose, sucrose, and fructan in the stem and sheath are remobilized to the spike through the UI, which ultimately affects grain plumpness [53, 54]. In addition, a longer UI may inhibit the reproduction of pathogens such as Fusarium by enhancing airflow around the spikes and reducing humidity [15]. Therefore, an optimal UI would enhance lodging resistance while maximizing light utilization, thereby eventually contributing to wheat yield.

Understanding the correlations among plant height-related traits is essential for balancing their relationship in wheat improvement. Our findings revealed a significant positive correlation between PH and PHCs, with LI3 contributing most to PH, as well as positive correlations of both PH and UI with TGW, which aligned with previous studies [24, 55, 56]. There was a significant negative correlation between internode length and TGW [24]. However, we found a positive correlation between LI2, LI3, LI4, LI5, and TGW in modern cultivars, possibly due to differing genetic backgrounds. Thus, in future breeding programs, wheat plant architecture can be optimized and yield regulated through judicious internode configuration.

sec.title: Application of SCVs in wheat breeding
sec.p: The use of SSR and SNP markers has become prevalent in GWAS and QTL analysis for the identification of loci associated with PH [26–28]. As an important source of genetic variation, SV is worthy of further investigation [31]. Notably, the application of ONPM FISH technology has provided a novel marker for the exploration of beneficial loci. A total of four SCVs showed significant association with PH [33]. This study identified 19 SCVs at 230 loci in a natural population and explained 4.2–9.3% of phenotypic variation. Among these, Mr2A-9 was significantly associated with SEL and LI3, which was close to the locus B-SIL-2A-1 for the LI2 reported by Liu et al. [17]. Mr2B-12 had significant effects on seven plant height-related traits except SL. This locus was found within a QTL enrichment cluster (688.6 Mb−703.3 Mb) that is implicated in the regulation of PH [57, 58]. Moreover, the observed increase in the frequency of favorable SCVs across release years indicated the positive selection applied in breeding programs. In the natural population, the co-located locus QSL.sxau-7B.1 (Mr7B-13) for the SL was close to wsnp_Ex_rep_c101269_86664147 which reported by Guo et al. [44] using a 9 K SNP array. Meanwhile, we verified the genetic effect of SCVs in the DH population, demonstrating the association between SCV polymorphism and PH regulation.

Modern breeding had significantly promoted the accumulation of favorable SNPs [59]. We analyzed the frequency of SNPs and SCVs significantly associated with eight plant height-related traits and found that the frequency of their favorable allelic variations in modern cultivars was significantly higher than that in landraces. It is noted that the favored allelic variation of QPH.sxau-1 A, QSL.sxau-6B, QSL.sxau-7B.1, 4AS‧4AL-1DS, 1DL·1DS-4AL, QLI3.sxau-7A, and Mr3B-7 remained a lower level in modern cultivars, indicating that the selection for these loci would be plausible in breeding programs. Additionally, 106 cultivars carried at least five favorable allelic variations associated with PH, accounting for 37.7% of the total cultivars (Fig. 4b). These cultivars may serve as valuable germplasm for improving wheat PH. Furthermore, the increase of favored SCVs corresponded to the elongated SL but the decreasing measurement of the internode length, indicating the significant additive effect. Interestingly, the loci identified by SNPs and SCVs also exhibited an additive effect. These results further support the potential application of SCVs as a new marker type in MAS breeding. Recently, high-quality genomes at the chromosomal level for 17 representative Chinese cultivars have become available, revealing nearly 250,000 SVs [31]. It is essential to determine the genetic effects of these SVs. In the future, SCV markers can be developed using repetitive sequences in conjunction with Oligo-FISH technology, thus enabling the application of SVs in MAS breeding.

sec.title: QPH.sxau-2A is a novel QTL for PH
sec.p: Previous studies mainly focused on localizing QTL for PH. The loci associated with PH have been identified on 21 chromosomes. At present, 27 dwarfing genes had been officially named [3]. This study detected 22 stable QTL for PH and PHCs, 17 of which are consistent with previously reported regions (Table 1). It is evident that the reliability of the results of this study. The QPH.sxau-2D for PH, represented by SNP 2D_32970833 at the position close to Rht8 [4], was detected in E4, E5, and BLUP datasets. Additionally, the QPH.sxau-1A coincided with the PH association loci Chr1A-B38-Hap3 reported by Luján et al. [39]. The QPH.sxau-6D was located near the PH association loci QHt.inra-6d (383.7 Mb) detected by Gervais et al. [41]. A total of 13 loci for PHCs located at the same position as or close to previously reported regions. For example, QLI2.sxau-4B and QLI3.sxau-4B were close to QPH.caas-4BS identified by Li et al. [57] in three RIL populations, which contained Rht1 [60]. Moreover, QLI3.sxau-2D and QLI4.sxau-2D have shared the same physical location as the peak marker of QPH.sxau-2D, which contained Rht8 [4]. In addition, the Rht1 was detected in UI and LI4. The loci QLI2.sxau-2B and QLI4.sxau-5D were close to Rht4 and Rht23, respectively [61, 62]. The loci QLI3.sxau-4D, QLI4.sxau-4D, and QLI5.sxau-4D (represented by SNP 4D_19090268) were located near the position of Rht10 [63]. These loci exhibited significant effects in as few as one or two experimental environments (Supplemental Table S5), probably because of gene-environment interactions and the complexity of genetic regulation for PH. This complexity necessitates further verification across diverse populations. The identified loci in this study would be useful for subsequent gene fine mapping and molecular marker development, potentially serving as gene resources for improving PH.

Moreover, we identified potentially novel locus QPH.sxau-2A, which was validated within the RIL population. The frequency of favored allelic variation in landraces was 92.1%, while the frequencies in dryland cultivars and the irrigated cultivars were 40.2% and 50.4%, respectively. The significant differences were observed between the two allelic variations within each cultivar type (Supplemental Fig. S7c). This locus not only reduced PH, but also significantly increased GNS, TGW, and GY. In addition, the locus QLI5.sxau-1B (Mg1B-1), which was co-localized with SNPs and SCVs and was positioned similarly to QPH-1B-wmc85, was mapped to LI5 in this study [45]. The favored allelic variation at this locus reduced LI5 while increasing GNS, TGW, and GY. Consequently, QPH.sxau-2A and QLI5.sxau-1B hold substantial promise for wheat breeding, as they not only mitigate lodging risk but also maintain robust biomass accumulation. Prioritizing these loci in upcoming PH improvement initiatives will be critical for balancing lodging resistance and productivity in modern cultivars.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: The PH gradually decreased across years of release, but there were differences in the selection pressure on each component of plant height, among which the uppermost internode length decreased the fastest. Genotype is the primary factor affecting plant height-related traits, and LI3 contributes more significantly to PH. In this study, based on the association analysis of SNPs and SCVs, 14 MTAs were co-located, among which QSL.sxau-7B.1 (Mr7B-13) was further verified in the DH population (Jinchun 7 × Jinmai 919). The accumulation of favorable SNPs and SCVs not only increased SL but also reduced PH and internode length. A novel PH locus, QPH.sxau-2A, was identified. Through fine mapping, the interval was narrowed to 41.8 Mb, with three candidate genes initially screened. These results provide comprehensive information for further genetic analysis and molecular breeding of wheat plant height-related traits.
